reports.title: Bass Angler Smashes Personal Best Twice in One Day
reports.text:
Ryan Park knew he was rolling the dice when he left Charlotte in search of a lake he had never fished before. He met up half way with one of his old college fishing partners that left from Tennessee. The trip came together after the two had spent weeks digging through online articles and social media posts about a little-known public lake in southeast Florida. The nameless lake had the reputation of producing giant largemouth bass. Between the gas, the time off work and the long drive down, the friends were, as Park put it, “betting the house on this lake producing.”

reports.title: Tournament Angler’s Last Cast is a Bittersweet Trip on a Lake Filled With Fishing Memories
reports.text:
One last cast.
For many anglers, that’s a common refrain at the end of a fishing trip.
For David Shaw, it had deeper meaning on a hot summer evening at Smithville Lake in northwest Missouri.
He was dying of cancer when he joined his son Tyler for what he sensed would be the last cast of his illustrious career.
A Lake Full of Memories
David Shaw liked traveling to the Northland to fish for big smallmouth bass. Photo courtesy of Tyler Shaw.
The father-son duo had dominated local and regional bass tournaments at Smithville Lake for some time. Now they were back for David, 76, to say goodbye.

reports.title: Mystery Bass Die Off At California Lake Traced To Largemouth Bass Virus
reports.text:
Lake of the Pines is a quiet, private 232-acre lake tucked into the foothills of Nevada County, California, and by most accounts its bass fishing was right on the mark. Residents were recently told the lake was in the best condition it had ever been in, and local anglers were bragging about catching four or five largemouth bass in an hour.
That changed in early September, when residents watched crews on a pontoon boat scoop dead fish off the water and bag them up. Ron Bonhoff, a former Lake of the Pines president who has lived on the lake for more than 40 years, said the sight caught him off guard.

reports.title: Success Lake remained at a very low water level
reports.text: Anglers caught quality largemouth bass near submerged trees, main-lake points, and the dam. Crappie fishing was fair to good on small minnows and minijigs around submerged brush.

reports.title: Fishing remained surprisingly good as fish concentrated in the main basin
reports.text: The spotted bass bite was good around main-lake points, steep drop-offs, and submerged rock piles in 15 to 25 feet of water, with drop-shots, Ned rigs, and shaky heads in natural colors producing the best results. Crappie fishing was fair to good on small minnows and jigs around remaining brush in 15 to 20 feet of water.

reports.title: The fall bite was in full effect for striped bass last week
reports.text: Largemouth bass were caught on drop-shot rigs with 4-inch plastic worms in brown and dark green, while soft jerkbaits also proved effective.

reports.title: Rare “Golden Burbot” Plucked From The Depths
reports.text:
Most anglers have seen their share of unusual catches, but this one might be tough to top.
Biologists with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) recently pulled a remarkably colored burbot from Oswego Harbor, New York. Instead of the usual brown and olive tones, this fish was sporting a bright yellow-orange color that looked more like a Halloween pumpkin than a bottom-dwelling Great Lakes fish.
The unusual coloration is known as xanthochromism, a rare pigmentation condition generally associated with genetic changes that produce yellow or orange coloring. And while oddly colored fish occasionally turn up in anglers’ catches, finding one like this in the wild is a pretty special…

reports.title: Thankfulness: so much to be thankful for
reports.text:
Cooler temperatures are just one reason to be thankful
N ovember is a month I’m thankful to see roll around every year. The cooler temperatures and frosty mornings are a reprieve from the intense heat domes we’ve suffered through these past summers. July and August triple-digit readings have forced me to sweat profusely instead of lightly perspiring. It’s wonderful to stand in cold water, chilled, and try to catch a trout on a fly. Exhaling slowly, I watch my damp breath turn into ice crystals and disappear. What a beautiful morning to be here. Quiet, alone, and time to ponder the things I’ve been too busy to think about otherwise.

reports.title: CN How To Nov 2026 How To: Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie behavior.
reports.text:
How To: Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie behavior.
In this episode of The Playbook, Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie and bass behavior. Fish often face into the current, positioning themselves where baitfish will naturally approach. During sunny conditions, they tend to hold in the shade created by stumps, brush, overhanging trees, and shoreline drop-offs, often near the edge of the light.
The key to success is proper boat positioning and bait placement. When casting or jigging, position your bait up current so it moves naturally toward the fish. Approaching from behind can spook them…

reports.text:
November is prime time for catching slab crappie. Knowing where fish
move as water temperatures fall can help beginners find more of them.
Crappie Basics: Finding and Catching Crappie in Cold Weather
Story and photo by Keith Sutton
November can be one of the most productive months for crappie fishing. As summer’s heat fades and water temperatures drop, crappie begin changing their habits, often moving into locations where they can feed heavily before winter arrives. For anglers who know how to follow these seasonal movements, some of the year’s biggest catches may be just around the corner.

reports.title: Hit Lake Murray’s brush for fall crappie
reports.text:
Don’t miss the fall crappie bite
A s Lake Murray’s water temperature cools down in October, Capt. Brad Taylor of Taylor Outdoors said the crappie fishing gets cranked up.
“October is a great month because you can catch crappie in a number of ways, really just about any way you want to catch them will work,” he said.
One way Taylor targets them this time of year is by fishing brush in the main river channel.
“Fall is kind of a magical time of year for Lake Murray because the shad start working up the river,” he said. “And the crappie follow the bait. If you can find the bait, which isn’t too difficult using electronics, then you can find the crappie.”

Paddlin’ with Madalyn: Stay Safe, Be Seen
by Madalyn Roberts
Before taking a kayak out on the water, be sure to familiarize yourself with the light requirements for your setup. From sunset to sunrise—and during other times of restricted visibility such as rain or heavy fog—kayaks that are paddled by hand or pedal-powered require some type of flashing white light. Motorized kayaks require both a continuously visible, 360-degree white light pole on the stern and standard navigation lights on the bow, red on port (left) and green on starboard (right).

reports.title: Crappie Basics: Match the Hatch for More Crappie
reports.text:
Matching your jig to the size and shape of the main crappie forage can greatly increase your number of hookups.
Crappie Basics: Match the Hatch for More Crappie
By Keith Sutton
One of the simplest ways to improve your crappie fishing is to give the fish what they’re already looking for. That means matching your jig to the size and general shape of the forage crappie are feeding on.
If 2-inch minnows make up a big part of the crappie diet in the lake you’re fishing, for example, a 2-inch jig is a logical choice. If the fish are eating tiny shiners, you’ll probably do better with a smaller offering. The same principle applies when shad, fathead minnows or other forage dominate the menu.
